items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Franz Boas's approach that each culture is the product of its own particular history and must be studied on its own terms"?
items.answer: historical particularism
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of historical particularism.

items.stem: Explain why unilineal evolutionism has been rejected by modern anthropologists.
items.answer: It ranked societies on a single scale with Europe at the top, assumed a fixed sequence that ethnography contradicts, ignored the histories and connections of peoples, and justified colonial rule.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It ranked societies on a single scale with Europe at the top, assumed a fixed sequence that ethnography contradicts, ignored the histories and connections of peoples, and justified colonial rule. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between diffusionism and independent invention.
items.answer: Diffusionism explains similar traits by borrowing and migration from a common source; independent invention explains them as separate responses arising in different places.
items.markingKey: Diffusionism explains similar traits by borrowing and migration from a common source; independent invention explains them as separate responses arising in different places. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Boas believed that cultures could be ranked from simple to complex." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Boas rejected ranking cultures and argued that each must be understood in its own historical context.
items.markingKey: Boas rejected ranking cultures and argued that each must be understood in its own historical context. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline how classification shapes early explanations of cultural difference, using evidence from Boas's historical particularism.
items.answer: His study of immigrants' children showed head shape changing within one generation in the United States, challenging fixed racial classifications.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: His study of immigrants' children showed head shape changing within one generation in the United States, challenging fixed racial classifications. Award up to [4]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Franz Boas's historical particularism (e.g. "The Limitations of the Comparative Method of Anthropology", 1896), in his work on the Kwakwaka'wakw of British Columbia and on immigrants in New York); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to classification. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Nineteenth-century evolutionism has nothing to offer anthropology today."
items.answer: Its racist ranking must be rejected, but its comparative ambition and some data remain useful.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: its ranking of societies was ethnocentric and served colonialism; ethnography refuted fixed stages. Arguments against: it asked big comparative questions about long-term change; Morgan founded kinship studies; neo-evolutionists (White, Steward) developed more careful models of cultural ecology. Supported judgement: Its racist ranking must be rejected, but its comparative ambition and some data remain useful.

items.stem: In Ancient Society (1877), Lewis Henry Morgan divided human history into which stages?
items.answer: Savagery, barbarism and civilisation
items.markingKey: C. Morgan's scheme ranked societies by technological inventions.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the regional museum, the 1930s display still stands in the hall: glass cases arranged in a line from "Stone Age Hunters" through "Primitive Farmers" to "Modern Civilisation", which ends with a model of a steam train. Schoolchildren walk past it on the way to the cafe. The new curator, Dr Achieng, has added handwritten cards: "These people were our grandparents' neighbours, not our ancestors from the Stone Age." A teacher told me she uses the display "to show how wrong we used to be". The museum board has not yet agreed to remove it.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a regional museum in East Africa.

Identify and describe how the museum display is arranged and used. Refer closely to the text. Focus on what the people in the text do and say, not on your interpretation of it.
items.answer: Glass cases arranged in a line from "Stone Age Hunters" to "Primitive Farmers" to "Modern Civilisation", ending with a steam train; schoolchildren pass on the way to the cafe; the curator has added handwritten cards challenging it; a teacher uses it to show past errors; the board has not agreed to remove it.
items.markingKey: Glass cases arranged in a line from "Stone Age Hunters" to "Primitive Farmers" to "Modern Civilisation", ending with a steam train; schoolchildren pass on the way to the cafe; the curator has added handwritten cards challenging it; a teacher uses it to show past errors; the board has not agreed to remove it. Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem: Radcliffe-Brown compared society to:
items.answer: a living organism whose parts maintain the whole
items.markingKey: a living organism whose parts maintain the whole. The organic analogy is central to structural-functionalism.

items.stem: Briefly explain why Evans-Pritchard's The Nuer is often seen as a structural-functionalist ethnography.
items.answer: It shows how segmentary lineages, age-sets and feud mechanisms maintain order without a state, explaining institutions by their contribution to social structure.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It shows how segmentary lineages, age-sets and feud mechanisms maintain order without a state, explaining institutions by their contribution to social structure. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between Radcliffe-Brown's structural-functionalism and Malinowski's functionalism.
items.answer: Malinowski explained institutions by the individual biological and psychological needs they satisfy; Radcliffe-Brown explained them by their role in maintaining the social structure as a whole.
items.markingKey: Malinowski explained institutions by the individual biological and psychological needs they satisfy; Radcliffe-Brown explained them by their role in maintaining the social structure as a whole. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which Evans-Pritchard's The Nuer (1940) shows structural-functionalism.
items.answer: Nuer lineages fused against outsiders and split in internal disputes, with leopard-skin chiefs mediating feuds. The segmentary system is analysed as maintaining order without a state, explaining institutions by their contribution to social structure.
items.markingKey: Context (Nuer lineages fused against outsiders and split in internal disputes, with leopard-skin chiefs mediating feuds.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the segmentary system is analysed as maintaining order without a state, explaining institutions by their contribution to social structure. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to structural-functionalism.

items.stem: A student claims: "Functionalism has no influence on anthropology today." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Its emphasis on holism, fieldwork and the interconnection of institutions remains central, even though its equilibrium model has been abandoned.
items.markingKey: Its emphasis on holism, fieldwork and the interconnection of institutions remains central, even though its equilibrium model has been abandoned. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the village, every household sends a son to the annual repair of the irrigation channel. Nobody is paid. The work lasts three days and ends with a feast at which the eldest man of each lineage receives the first portion of meat. Thabo, home from his job in Johannesburg, paid a cousin to go in his place this year. The elders accepted the money but placed Thabo's family last in the line for the feast. "The channel brings water to all," the headman told me. "When a family does not dig, the water still comes, but the respect does not."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a rural village in Lesotho.

With reference to the concept of society, analyse how a functionalist might explain the channel repair, and what the text suggests about the limits of that explanation. Distinguish between what the text shows and what you infer from it.
items.answer: A functionalist would argue the collective work meets the material need for water (Malinowski) and maintains social structure and solidarity, with the feast reaffirming lineage seniority (Radcliffe-Brown). But Thabo's substitution shows change from migrant wage labour and money entering obligations, and the sanction on his family shows tension and negotiation that an equilibrium model underplays.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: A functionalist would argue the collective work meets the material need for water (Malinowski) and maintains social structure and solidarity, with the feast reaffirming lineage seniority (Radcliffe-Brown). But Thabo's substitution shows change from migrant wage labour and money entering obligations, and the sanction on his family shows tension and negotiation that an equilibrium model underplays. Markbands – 5–6: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 3–4: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1–2: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that functionalism presents an overly harmonious picture of society? Answer with reference to one ethnography in depth.
items.answer: Functionalism did often over-emphasise harmony, but later functionalists began to analyse conflict and its holistic insights endure.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: the equilibrium model treats conflict as dysfunction; it ignored colonial power that shaped the societies studied; it struggles with change; Max Gluckman (Manchester School) showed conflict can be functional, e.g. rituals of rebellion; its holism explained how institutions interconnect. Suitable ethnographies include Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific, Radcliffe-Brown's structural-functionalism, Evans-Pritchard's The Nuer. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Functionalism did often over-emphasise harmony, but later functionalists began to analyse conflict and its holistic insights endure. Evaluate the ethical challenges of researching, writing and publishing an account such as the one in the text. You may refer to ethical codes, but apply them to the situation described.

items.stem: Briefly explain why functionalism was an advance over evolutionism.
items.answer: It explained institutions by their present role in a living society, based on fieldwork, rather than as survivals from earlier stages, and it showed that apparently strange customs made sense in context.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It explained institutions by their present role in a living society, based on fieldwork, rather than as survivals from earlier stages, and it showed that apparently strange customs made sense in context. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to one ethnography you have studied, for example Evans-Pritchard's Witchcraft, Oracles and Magic among the Azande, explain the relevance of social relations to the maintenance of social order.
items.answer: Witchcraft accusations follow tensions between neighbours and rivals, and consulting the poison oracle (benge) channels conflict into a recognised procedure.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Witchcraft accusations follow tensions between neighbours and rivals, and consulting the poison oracle (benge) channels conflict into a recognised procedure. Award up to [3]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (E. E. Evans-Pritchard, Witchcraft, Oracles and Magic among the Azande (1937), among the Azande of the southern Sudan (fieldwork 1926–1930)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to social relations. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: Using Radcliffe-Brown's structural-functionalism and Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific, compare the ways in which social relations is experienced and contested by the people studied.
items.answer: Radcliffe-Brown's structural-functionalism (drawing on fieldwork in the Andaman Islands (1906–1908) and comparative work on African and Australian kinship): In "The Mother's Brother in South Africa" (1924) he explained joking and respect relationships by the structural positions of kin rather than by historical survivals. Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific (among the Trobriand Islanders of Papua New Guinea (fieldwork 1915–1918)): In the kula ring, men on different islands keep lifelong partnerships through the ceremonial exchange of shell valuables: soulava necklaces travel clockwise and mwali armshells anticlockwise, creating alliances between communities rather than profit. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far social relations is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Radcliffe-Brown's structural-functionalism (drawing on fieldwork in the Andaman Islands (1906–1908) and comparative work on African and Australian kinship): In "The Mother's Brother in South Africa" (1924) he explained joking and respect relationships by the structural positions of kin rather than by historical survivals. Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific (among the Trobriand Islanders of Papua New Guinea (fieldwork 1915–1918)): In the kula ring, men on different islands keep lifelong partnerships through the ceremonial exchange of shell valuables: soulava necklaces travel clockwise and mwali armshells anticlockwise, creating alliances between communities rather than profit. items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "multivocality".
items.answer: Victor Turner's term for the capacity of a dominant symbol to carry many meanings at once
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: Victor Turner's term for the capacity of a dominant symbol to carry many meanings at once. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: "Thick description means writing very long, detailed accounts of behaviour." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Thick description means interpreting the layered meanings of actions in context, not merely adding detail.
items.markingKey: Thick description means interpreting the layered meanings of actions in context, not merely adding detail. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between thin description and thick description.
items.answer: Thin description records observable behaviour (a contraction of the eyelid); thick description interprets its meaning in context (a wink, a parody of a wink), which requires understanding the cultural codes involved.
items.markingKey: Thin description records observable behaviour (a contraction of the eyelid); thick description interprets its meaning in context (a wink, a parody of a wink), which requires understanding the cultural codes involved. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which Turner's analysis of the Ndembu milk tree (mudyi) shows multivocal symbols.
items.answer: The milk tree, which exudes white latex, is central in girls' puberty rites. The tree stands simultaneously for breast milk, motherhood, matrilineal descent and Ndembu unity, showing how one symbol condenses many meanings.
items.markingKey: Context (The milk tree, which exudes white latex, is central in girls' puberty rites.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the tree stands simultaneously for breast milk, motherhood, matrilineal descent and Ndembu unity, showing how one symbol condenses many meanings. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to multivocal symbols.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

At the wedding in Izmir, the bride's family serves rice with pine nuts and the groom's family brings roasted lamb. Aunt Fatma explains: "Rice is for the house, meat is for the guests." The henna night before the wedding is only for women; the bride's hands are painted while the older women sing laments about a daughter leaving her mother. The bride, Elif, a software engineer, laughed during the songs, then cried. "I live ten minutes away," she told me. "But tonight I am leaving forever."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a wedding in western Turkey.

Describe, with examples from the text, the food and ritual practices described in the text. You do not need to refer to any other ethnography in this answer.
items.answer: The bride's family serves rice with pine nuts; the groom's family brings roasted lamb; Fatma says rice is for the house and meat for guests; the henna night is for women only; the bride's hands are painted while older women sing laments; Elif laughed and then cried.

Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.

items.stem: Briefly explain why Geertz argued that anthropology is "not an experimental science in search of law but an interpretive one in search of meaning".
items.answer: Human action is meaningful within a culture's webs of significance; the task is to interpret what actions mean to those involved, like reading a text, rather than to discover universal laws.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Human action is meaningful within a culture's webs of significance; the task is to interpret what actions mean to those involved, like reading a text, rather than to discover universal laws. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

Explain, with close reference to the text, how a structuralist and an interpretive anthropologist might each analyse the wedding. Link the actions described to wider social, economic or political conditions.
items.answer: A structuralist would identify binary oppositions: rice/meat, house/guests, bride's side/groom's side, women's henna night/public wedding, staying/leaving – mental structures organising the ritual. An interpretive anthropologist would read the henna night as a text about a daughter's transition, using Elif's laughter and tears and her words ("tonight I am leaving forever") to interpret its emotional, symbolic meaning despite living ten minutes away.

items.stem: Who wrote Europe and the People Without History (1982)?
items.answer: Eric Wolf
items.markingKey: C. Wolf traced the integration of the world's peoples into capitalism.

items.stem: Distinguish between agency and structure.
items.answer: Structure is the set of enduring social patterns and constraints; agency is the capacity of people to act and change them. Practice theory sees each as produced through the other.
items.markingKey: Structure is the set of enduring social patterns and constraints; agency is the capacity of people to act and change them. Practice theory sees each as produced through the other. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Practice theory claims that individuals are completely free to choose their actions." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Practice theory stresses that action is shaped by habitus and structure, even though it can also reproduce or transform them.
items.markingKey: Practice theory stresses that action is shaped by habitus and structure, even though it can also reproduce or transform them. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Identify one way in which identity matters in Ortner's essay "Is Female to Male as Nature Is to Culture?" (in a comparative feminist analysis of gender symbolism across societies) and explain its significance.
items.answer: Gender identity is a cultural construction: nothing in biology dictates women's lower status; the nature/culture association is symbolic and could change.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Gender identity is a cultural construction: nothing in biology dictates women's lower status; the nature/culture association is symbolic and could change. Award up to [3]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Sherry Ortner, "Is Female to Male as Nature Is to Culture?" (Feminist Studies, 1972; reprinted 1974 in Woman, Culture, and Society), in a comparative feminist analysis of gender symbolism across societies); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to identity. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

At the call centre in Pune, the trainers teach new staff to "neutralise" their accents and to choose an English name for the night shift. Rohan becomes "Ryan" at 9 p.m. The best performers win vouchers for coffee shops where, Rohan tells me, he would not have felt comfortable two years ago. His father, a retired railway clerk, calls the job "selling your sleep to America". Rohan sends half his salary home and has bought his mother a washing machine. "Ryan pays for it," he laughs, "Rohan enjoys it."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a call centre in India.

Identify and describe the changes the call centre job brings to Rohan's life. Refer closely to the text. You do not need to refer to any other ethnography in this answer.
items.answer: He trains to neutralise his accent and uses the name "Ryan" on the night shift; he wins vouchers and feels comfortable in coffee shops he previously avoided; he sends half his salary home and bought his mother a washing machine; his father criticises the job as "selling your sleep to America".
items.markingKey: He trains to neutralise his accent and uses the name "Ryan" on the night shift; he wins vouchers and feels comfortable in coffee shops he previously avoided; he sends half his salary home and bought his mother a washing machine; his father criticises the job as "selling your sleep to America". Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that marxist approaches explain culture better than interpretive approaches. Support your answer with ethnographic material and anthropological theory.
items.answer: Each explains different aspects; the strongest analyses combine meaning with political economy.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: they reveal inequality and global connections (Wolf); they explain change; they may reduce meaning to economics; interpretive approaches capture what practices mean to participants (Geertz). Suitable ethnographies include Wolf's Europe and the People Without History, Ortner's essay "Is Female to Male as Nature Is to Culture?", Bourdieu's Outline of a Theory of Practice. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Each explains different aspects; the strongest analyses combine meaning with political economy. items.stem: Briefly explain why Bourdieu's concept of habitus helps explain the reproduction of inequality.
items.answer: Habitus makes social dispositions feel natural, so people tend to act in ways that fit their position (e.g. "choosing" what is realistic), reproducing class and gender hierarchies without explicit coercion.

Compare the significance of power in the text with its significance in Scott's Weapons of the Weak. Refer explicitly to the ethnographic context of both. Your answer should identify both similarities and differences.
items.answer: Text: A Marxist approach highlights global capitalism: Indian workers sell labour time (night shifts) to US firms, and their accents and names are disciplined to serve foreign customers. Practice theory highlights how Rohan's habitus is reshaped (new tastes, cultural capital, comfort in coffee shops) and how he uses agency, splitting identities ("Ryan pays… Rohan enjoys") to gain resources for his family, partly reproducing and partly transforming class position. Ethnography – James C. Scott, Weapons of the Weak: Everyday Forms of Peasant Resistance (1985), in "Sedaka", a pseudonymous rice-growing village in Kedah, Malaysia (fieldwork 1978–1980): After double-cropping and combine harvesters cut work for poor villagers, they resisted through foot-dragging, gossip, pilfering and slander against rich farmers rather than open revolt. Comparison: similarities and differences in how power is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

Comparison: similarities and differences in how power is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them. Any well-contextualised ethnography is acceptable. items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "structural-functionalism".
items.answer: Radcliffe-Brown's theory that institutions function to maintain the social structure and the stability of society as a whole
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: Radcliffe-Brown's theory that institutions function to maintain the social structure and the stability of society as a whole. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "psychic unity of mankind"?
options: An approach, influenced by Marx, that analyses culture in relation to production, class and global relations of power and exchange
Franz Boas's approach that each culture is the product of its own particular history and must be studied on its own terms
The idea, held by evolutionists such as Tylor, that all humans share the same mental capacities, so similar stages arise independently
The nineteenth-century theory that all societies progress through the same fixed sequence of stages, from "savagery" to "civilisation"
items.answer: The idea, held by evolutionists such as Tylor, that all humans share the same mental capacities, so similar stages arise independently
items.markingKey: C. "psychic unity of mankind" is the idea, held by evolutionists such as Tylor, that all humans share the same mental capacities, so similar stages arise independently.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Victor Turner's term for the capacity of a dominant symbol to carry many meanings at once"?
items.answer: multivocality
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of multivocality.

items.stem: "Feminist anthropology is only about studying women." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Feminist anthropology analyses gender as a system of power affecting everyone, including masculinity, and questions male bias in theory and method.
items.markingKey: Feminist anthropology analyses gender as a system of power affecting everyone, including masculinity, and questions male bias in theory and method. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Functionalists believed every custom is good for every individual." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Functionalists claimed institutions contribute to social stability or meet needs, not that they benefit everyone; critics note that the theory can hide inequality.
items.markingKey: Functionalists claimed institutions contribute to social stability or meet needs, not that they benefit everyone; critics note that the theory can hide inequality. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Evolutionist anthropologists based their theories on long-term fieldwork." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Most were "armchair" scholars who relied on reports by missionaries, traders and administrators; Morgan was a partial exception with his Haudenosaunee work.
items.markingKey: Most were "armchair" scholars who relied on reports by missionaries, traders and administrators; Morgan was a partial exception with his Haudenosaunee work. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why interpretive anthropology has been criticised for neglecting power.
items.answer: By treating culture as a shared text, it can ignore who controls meanings, whose interpretations prevail and how symbols serve inequality; Talal Asad and William Roseberry raised such criticisms.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: By treating culture as a shared text, it can ignore who controls meanings, whose interpretations prevail and how symbols serve inequality; Talal Asad and William Roseberry raised such criticisms. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Practice theory claims that individuals are completely free to choose their actions." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Practice theory stresses that action is shaped by habitus and structure, even though it can also reproduce or transform them.
items.markingKey: Practice theory stresses that action is shaped by habitus and structure, even though it can also reproduce or transform them. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a synchronic approach and a diachronic approach.
items.answer: A synchronic approach studies a society as a system at one moment; a diachronic approach studies it through time, emphasising history and change.
items.markingKey: A synchronic approach studies a society as a system at one moment; a diachronic approach studies it through time, emphasising history and change. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the regional museum, the 1930s display still stands in the hall: glass cases arranged in a line from "Stone Age Hunters" through "Primitive Farmers" to "Modern Civilisation", which ends with a model of a steam train. Schoolchildren walk past it on the way to the cafe. The new curator, Dr Achieng, has added handwritten cards: "These people were our grandparents' neighbours, not our ancestors from the Stone Age." A teacher told me she uses the display "to show how wrong we used to be". The museum board has not yet agreed to remove it.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a regional museum in East Africa.

Analyse how the display reflects nineteenth-century evolutionist thinking and how it is being challenged. Support your answer with evidence from the text. You may consider more than one possible interpretation of the evidence.
items.answer: The linear sequence ranks contemporary peoples as earlier stages of humanity and places industrial Europe (the train) at the summit – classic unilineal evolutionism. The curator's cards insist these peoples were contemporaries (coeval), in the spirit of Boas and Wolf; the teacher turns the display into a lesson about the history of ideas, while the board's reluctance shows institutional power over representation.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The linear sequence ranks contemporary peoples as earlier stages of humanity and places industrial Europe (the train) at the summit – classic unilineal evolutionism. The curator's cards insist these peoples were contemporaries (coeval), in the spirit of Boas and Wolf; the teacher turns the display into a lesson about the history of ideas, while the board's reluctance shows institutional power over representation. items.stem: Outline how classification shapes the meanings of myth, ritual and symbols, using evidence from Douglas's Purity and Danger.
items.answer: Douglas argued that dirt is "matter out of place": ideas of pollution arise wherever a system of classification produces anomalies that do not fit its categories.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Douglas argued that dirt is "matter out of place": ideas of pollution arise wherever a system of classification produces anomalies that do not fit its categories. Award up to [4]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Mary Douglas, Purity and Danger (1966), drawing on her fieldwork among the Lele of the Kasai (Democratic Republic of the Congo) and on the dietary rules of Leviticus); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to classification. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Bourdieu's analysis of the Kabyle house shows habitus and the embodiment of power.
items.answer: The house is divided by oppositions such as light/dark, high/low, male/female, and daily movement through it follows these divisions. Children absorb the gender order through bodily routines in space, so domination becomes taken for granted.
items.markingKey: Context (The house is divided by oppositions such as light/dark, high/low, male/female, and daily movement through it follows these divisions.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: children absorb the gender order through bodily routines in space, so domination becomes taken for granted. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to habitus and the embodiment of power.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the village, every household sends a son to the annual repair of the irrigation channel. Nobody is paid. The work lasts three days and ends with a feast at which the eldest man of each lineage receives the first portion of meat. Thabo, home from his job in Johannesburg, paid a cousin to go in his place this year. The elders accepted the money but placed Thabo's family last in the line for the feast. "The channel brings water to all," the headman told me. "When a family does not dig, the water still comes, but the respect does not."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a rural village in Lesotho.

Using evidence from the text, describe what happens during the annual repair of the irrigation channel. You do not need to refer to any other ethnography in this answer.
items.answer: Every household sends a son; the work is unpaid and lasts three days; it ends with a feast; the eldest man of each lineage receives the first portion; Thabo paid a cousin to go in his place; his family was placed last in the line for the feast.
items.markingKey: Every household sends a son; the work is unpaid and lasts three days; it ends with a feast; the eldest man of each lineage receives the first portion; Thabo paid a cousin to go in his place; his family was placed last in the line for the feast. Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem: Using Morgan's research with the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) as an example, explain evolutionism.
items.answer: Morgan studied Seneca kinship and political organisation and compared kinship terminologies worldwide. His data were valuable, but he fitted societies into a sequence of stages, ranking the Haudenosaunee in "barbarism", illustrating the strengths and flaws of evolutionism.
items.markingKey: Context (Morgan studied Seneca kinship and political organisation and compared kinship terminologies worldwide.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: his data were valuable, but he fitted societies into a sequence of stages, ranking the Haudenosaunee in "barbarism", illustrating the strengths and flaws of evolutionism. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to evolutionism.

items.stem: Sana writes: "Structuralists studied what individual people consciously think about their myths." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Structuralists sought unconscious structures of thought that people are usually unaware of, revealed by comparing many myths.
items.markingKey: Structuralists sought unconscious structures of thought that people are usually unaware of, revealed by comparing many myths. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

At the call centre in Pune, the trainers teach new staff to "neutralise" their accents and to choose an English name for the night shift. Rohan becomes "Ryan" at 9 p.m. The best performers win vouchers for coffee shops where, Rohan tells me, he would not have felt comfortable two years ago. His father, a retired railway clerk, calls the job "selling your sleep to America". Rohan sends half his salary home and has bought his mother a washing machine. "Ryan pays for it," he laughs, "Rohan enjoys it."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a call centre in India.

With reference to the concept of power, analyse how Marxist and practice-theory approaches could analyse Rohan's experience. Support each step of your explanation with evidence from the extract.
items.answer: A Marxist approach highlights global capitalism: Indian workers sell labour time (night shifts) to US firms, and their accents and names are disciplined to serve foreign customers. Practice theory highlights how Rohan's habitus is reshaped (new tastes, cultural capital, comfort in coffee shops) and how he uses agency, splitting identities ("Ryan pays… Rohan enjoys") to gain resources for his family, partly reproducing and partly transforming class position.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: A Marxist approach highlights global capitalism: Indian workers sell labour time (night shifts) to US firms, and their accents and names are disciplined to serve foreign customers. Practice theory highlights how Rohan's habitus is reshaped (new tastes, cultural capital, comfort in coffee shops) and how he uses agency, splitting identities ("Ryan pays… Rohan enjoys") to gain resources for his family, partly reproducing and partly transforming class position. items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Malinowski's contribution to method was more important than his theory."
items.answer: His methodological legacy is greater, though his theory shaped how that method was used.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: his model of long-term participant observation defines the discipline; his functionalist theory has been largely abandoned. Arguments against: his theory encouraged holistic analysis; method and theory were linked: needs-based theory led him to observe daily life. Supported judgement: His methodological legacy is greater, though his theory shaped how that method was used.

Evaluate the ethical challenges of researching, writing and publishing an account such as the one in the text. Suggest how the anthropologist might respond to the dilemmas you identify.
items.answer: Descendants of the people displayed may be offended; the anthropologist should seek consent from staff and consider how criticism of the board may affect the curator's position; representation of communities in the display raises questions of who should be consulted. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.

items.stem: "Structuralism tells us more about the anthropologist's mind than about the people studied." Discuss.
items.answer: Structuralism risks imposing analytic categories, but it provided powerful comparative insights.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: binary oppositions may be imposed by the analyst; it ignores emic meanings and history. Arguments against: comparative evidence shows recurring oppositions across cultures; it revealed logical patterns in myth and kinship that were not obvious. items.stem: "Ortner's nature/culture argument successfully explains gender inequality." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: It was influential but too universal; gender inequality must be explained in specific historical and cultural contexts.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it identified a widespread symbolic pattern; it stimulated feminist theory. Arguments against: the nature/culture opposition is itself a Western construct (MacCormack and Strathern, 1980); gender status varies widely (Weiner, Sanday); Ortner later revised her view. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "binary opposition"?
options: A pair of contrasting categories, such as nature/culture or raw/cooked, through which, according to structuralists, humans order experience
An approach, influenced by Marx, that analyses culture in relation to production, class and global relations of power and exchange
Eric Wolf's (from Marx) concept for the way labour is mobilised and organised, such as kin-ordered, tributary or capitalist
Pierre Bourdieu's term for the durable, embodied dispositions, acquired through upbringing, that shape how people perceive and act

items.stem: Explain the difference between Marxist anthropology and interpretive anthropology.
items.answer: Marxist anthropology explains culture through material production, class and power; interpretive anthropology explains culture as systems of meaning to be read; the first asks whose interests culture serves, the second what it means.
items.markingKey: Marxist anthropology explains culture through material production, class and power; interpretive anthropology explains culture as systems of meaning to be read; the first asks whose interests culture serves, the second what it means. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between Malinowski's functionalism and Radcliffe-Brown's structural-functionalism.
items.answer: Malinowski explained institutions by the individual biological and psychological needs they satisfy; Radcliffe-Brown explained them by their role in maintaining the social structure as a whole.
items.markingKey: Malinowski explained institutions by the individual biological and psychological needs they satisfy; Radcliffe-Brown explained them by their role in maintaining the social structure as a whole. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between independent invention and diffusionism.
items.answer: Diffusionism explains similar traits by borrowing and migration from a common source; independent invention explains them as separate responses arising in different places.
items.markingKey: Diffusionism explains similar traits by borrowing and migration from a common source; independent invention explains them as separate responses arising in different places. items.stem: Briefly explain why Marxist anthropologists insisted on the importance of history and global connection.
items.answer: They argued that local cultures are shaped by relations of production and by incorporation into capitalism, colonialism and trade, so analysing a society as isolated and timeless misses the causes of its forms and inequalities (Wolf).

items.stem: Briefly describe Geertz's "Deep Play" and explain what it reveals about interpretive anthropology.
items.answer: Geertz analysed the cockfight as a text in which Balinese men dramatise status rivalries. The cockfight is read as a symbolic story about status hierarchy rather than explained by function or gambling.

items.stem: Using Mead's Coming of Age in Samoa and Morgan's Ancient Society, compare the ways in which change is experienced and contested by the people studied.
items.answer: Mead's Coming of Age in Samoa (among adolescent girls on Ta'ū in the Manu'a Islands of American Samoa (fieldwork 1925–1926)): Mead used Samoa as a mirror to argue that American child-rearing and sexual norms could be changed, presenting ethnography as cultural critique of her own society. items.stem:
Read the text below.

At the call centre in Pune, the trainers teach new staff to "neutralise" their accents and to choose an English name for the night shift. Rohan becomes "Ryan" at 9 p.m. The best performers win vouchers for coffee shops where, Rohan tells me, he would not have felt comfortable two years ago. His father, a retired railway clerk, calls the job "selling your sleep to America". Rohan sends half his salary home and has bought his mother a washing machine. "Ryan pays for it," he laughs, "Rohan enjoys it."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a call centre in India.

Evaluate the ethical challenges of researching, writing and publishing an account such as the one in the text. Suggest how the anthropologist might respond to the dilemmas you identify.
items.answer: Employer surveillance and confidentiality agreements mean Rohan could lose his job if identified; the company should not be named without permission; family comments are private; consent should cover how his dual identity is presented. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.
